IEE Half-Day Colloquium on Lightning Protection of Wind Turbines (Digest No: 1997/303)
abstract: Total protection from lightning is not presently possible, however even if it was, it is likely that economic considerations would preclude universal application. The assessment of risk is therefore an essential element in the consideration of protection of any structure. The question of where, and how much, and what type of protection does not have an exact answer. The consequences of a strike need to be assessed and the costs of protection balanced against the cost of accepting the increased risk if protection is not installed. However, the risk cannot be evaluated without knowledge of the probability that a strike of a given strength will occur in the vicinity of the structure to be protected. This is the role of lightning location systems such as that operated by EA Technology. The author discusses the EA Technology lightning location system which uses radio direction finding techniques to locate lightning strikes as they occur. The system has been operated as a commercial service since 1989, providing both on-line information and historical information on lightning activity in the UK and Ireland. The isoceraunic level, ground stroke density, stroke strength, polarity and temporal variations are discussed.

abstract: This paper examines the use of computer modelling to assess the suitability of windfarm grounding systems for protection against power system faults and lightning strikes. The transient behaviour of practical earthing system designs are presented using the general purpose EMTP program and the specialist CDEGS grounding analysis software.

articleTitle: The effects of lightning on structures and establishing the level of risk
publicationTitle: IEE Half-Day Colloquium on Lightning Protection of Wind Turbines (Digest No: 1997/303)
abstract: The high levels of energy, current, charge and rate of current rise associated with a lightning strike can result in a structure being severely damaged if struck. A key stage in determining the type of lightning protection system (LPS) required by a structure is the estimation of the lightning strike frequency. For each strike, the probability of the energy/current/charge/rate of current rise exceeding a specific value can also be found mathematically. The IEC standard detailing lightning protection of structures, IEC 1024-1: 1990, provides a method of calculating the lightning strike frequency to an object of no more than 60 m height. Considering modern wind turbines may have a hub height greater than 60 m, this standard is inapplicable to such machines. Of particular importance in tall structures is the possibility of upward propagating lightning strikes. The assessment of the total lightning strike frequency, both upward and downward propagating, can be assessed using two independent models.

articleTitle: Protection of wind turbines control systems from the induced effects of lightning
publicationTitle: IEE Half-Day Colloquium on Lightning Protection of Wind Turbines (Digest No: 1997/303)
abstract: The control equipment installed in a wind turbine can be susceptible to induced voltage transients arising from a lightning strike. Transient levels are very dependent on small details of installation such as wire routing, and in this paper suggestions are made to minimise these lightning effects by simple installation procedures.

articleTitle: Lightning: safety and protection [wind power plants]
publicationTitle: IEE Half-Day Colloquium on Lightning Protection of Wind Turbines (Digest No: 1997/303)
abstract: Lightning to tall structures, such as wind turbine towers, power poles, etc., results in relatively high transient voltages. These lightning generated voltages can cause insulation failures and generate safety problems for humans and animals in the vicinity of the strike. This paper addresses the issues relative to these phenomena and describes a model for predicting lightning effects on a wind turbine/generator tower.

articleTitle: Overview of component damage by lightning and protection [wind turbines]
publicationTitle: IEE Half-Day Colloquium on Lightning Protection of Wind Turbines (Digest No: 1997/303)
abstract: This paper summarises the laboratory testing and field data obtained on wind turbine blades and bearings to date in the JOULE research programme. The conclusions presented are interim because work is still in progress. Blades are the second most likely item to be damaged in a lightning strike (after the electronics system) but the damage results in a much greater loss in output. Bearings, in contrast to blades, are often protected against lightning because they are on the path to ground and not too expensive to protect, rather than being seriously affected to any obvious extent.
